title: Ἀπόπλους εἰς Ἰθάκην
about: Odysseus has finished his tale, and the hall of Alcinous is spellbound. Alcinous answers that Odysseus will not be turned back again on his way home, and proposes that his lords add a tripod and a cauldron to the gifts already given, to be repaid by a levy on the people. The next morning the bronze is carried to the ship and stowed, and the day is spent in sacrifice and feasting, while Odysseus keeps looking at the sun and longs for it to set. At sunset he asks to be sent on his way, wishes the Phaeacians well, puts the cup into Arete’s hand and says farewell. A herald and servant women go with him to the ship, where a bed is laid for him in the stern, and the crew row out. He falls into an unwaking sleep, the ship runs on faster than a hawk, and before dawn she reaches the harbour of Phorcys in Ithaca, with its olive tree and its cave of the nymphs.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ,
κηληθμῷ δ’ ἔσχοντο κατὰ μέγαρα σκιόεντα.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence,
and were held by a spell throughout the shadowy halls.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent, held in a spell throughout the shadowy halls.
sentences.n: The narrator’s voice returns after Odysseus’s long tale, and the hall is seen to be bewitched by it. ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’; ἔφαθ’ is the past tense ἔφατο with its last vowel elided, and the τ is aspirated to θ before the rough breathing of οἱ. ἀκήν ‘still, hushed’ and σιωπῇ ‘in silence’ say nearly the same thing twice, for emphasis. κηληθμῷ is a dative, ‘by a spell’ (κηληθμός ‘enchantment’), and ἔσχοντο is the aorist middle of ἔχω, ‘were held’. κατὰ μέγαρα means ‘throughout the halls’; the plural μέγαρα is used of one great hall, and σκιόεντα ‘shadowy’ is built on σκιά ‘shadow’. The same hush and the same spell are given to Odysseus’s audience at 11.333–334.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀλκίνοος ἀπαμείβετο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.l: Him then in turn answered Alcinous, and spoke:
sentences.i: Then Alcinous answered him in turn, and spoke:
sentences.n: A standing formula of reply. τόν is the Homeric pronoun ‘him’, not the article; αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn’, elided. ἀπαμείβετο is ‘answered’ (ἀπο- + ἀμείβομαι ‘reply’), and φώνησεν is the aorist of φωνέω ‘speak’, the second verb. The same formula introduces Alcinous’s replies at 7.298 and 7.308. Alcinous is replying to the whole tale, and he speaks first as host.

sentences.t:
ὦ Ὀδυσεῦ, ἐπεὶ ἵκευ ἐμὸν ποτὶ χαλκοβατὲς δῶ,
ὑψερεφές, τῷ σ’ οὔ τι παλιμπλαγχθέντα γ’ ὀΐω
ἂψ ἀπονοστήσειν, εἰ καὶ μάλα πολλὰ πέπονθας.
sentences.l:
“O Odysseus, since you have come to my bronze-floored house,
high-roofed; therefore you, driven astray again, I do not at all think
will return back home, even if you have suffered very much.
sentences.i: “Odysseus, now that you have come to my house with its bronze floor, high-roofed as it is, I do not think you will be driven off course again on your way home, however much you have suffered.
sentences.n: Alcinous tells Odysseus that his wandering is over. Ὀδυσεῦ is the vocative of Ὀδυσσεύς with one σ. ἵκευ is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘come to’ without augment. ποτί is the Homeric form of πρός ‘to’, and δῶ is a short form of δῶμα ‘house’. χαλκοβατές ‘bronze-floored’ is built on βαίνω ‘step’; whether the bronze is the floor or the threshold is disputed. ὑψερεφές ‘high-roofed’ agrees with δῶ. τῷ is ‘therefore’. οὔ τι is ‘not at all’ and goes with ὀΐω ‘I think’, which takes an accusative and infinitive: σε … ἀπονοστήσειν ‘that you will return home’ (a future infinitive from νόστος ‘homecoming’). παλιμπλαγχθέντα is the aorist passive participle of the verb formed from πάλιν ‘back, again’ and πλάζω ‘drive astray’: ‘driven off course again’.

sentences.t:
ὑμέων δ’ ἀνδρὶ ἑκάστῳ ἐφιέμενος τάδε εἴρω,
ὅσσοι ἐνὶ μεγάροισι γερούσιον αἴθοπα οἶνον
αἰεὶ πίνετ’ ἐμοῖσιν, ἀκουάζεσθε δ’ ἀοιδοῦ.
sentences.l:
And to each man of you, enjoining it, I say this,
as many as in the halls the elders’ fire-faced wine
always drink in mine, and listen to the minstrel.
sentences.i: And this I urge on each man of you who always drink the elders’ wine that has the look of fire in my halls, and listen to the minstrel.
sentences.n: Alcinous now turns from Odysseus to his lords, and the sentence names whom he means before it says what he asks. ὑμέων is the uncontracted ὑμῶν ‘of you’, with ἀνδρὶ ἑκάστῳ ‘to each man’. ἐφιέμενος is from ἐφίεμαι ‘urge, lay a charge upon’, and τάδε ‘this’ looks forward to the proposal in lines 13–15. εἴρω ‘I say’ is an old present. ὅσσοι ‘as many as’ opens the relative clause: those who drink in his halls. γερούσιον means ‘of the elders’ (γέροντες), the wine of the council. αἴθοπα is from αἶθοψ, ‘fire-faced’ (αἴθω ‘burn’ + ὄψ ‘face, look’), built like οἶνοψ ‘wine-faced’. πίνετ’ is the second person plural, elided, and ἀκουάζεσθε takes the genitive ἀοιδοῦ: ‘listen to the minstrel’, who in Book 8 was Demodocus.

sentences.t:
εἵματα μὲν δὴ ξείνῳ ἐϋξέστῃ ἐνὶ χηλῷ
κεῖται καὶ χρυσὸς πολυδαίδαλος ἄλλα τε πάντα
δῶρ’, ὅσα Φαιήκων βουληφόροι ἐνθάδ’ ἔνεικαν·
sentences.i: Clothes and richly wrought gold lie ready for the stranger in a well-polished chest, and all the other gifts that the Phaeacian counsellors have brought here;
sentences.n: These are the guest-gifts already collected for Odysseus in Book 8, and Alcinous lists them before adding to them. εἵματα is a neuter plural, ‘clothes’, and the singular verb κεῖται ‘lies’ serves the whole list that follows: clothes, gold and the other gifts. ξείνῳ is the dative of the person concerned, ‘for the stranger’. ἐϋξέστῃ ‘well-polished’ agrees with χηλῷ ‘chest’. πολυδαίδαλος ‘much-wrought’ (πολυ- ‘many’ + δαίδαλος ‘cunningly made’) is the epithet used of a chamber at 6.15, and here it describes the gold. βουληφόροι is from βουλή ‘counsel’ and φέρω ‘bear’: the men who carry counsel in the assembly. ἔνεικαν is the aorist of φέρω without augment. The line ends with ·, the end of the sentence.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε οἱ δῶμεν τρίποδα μέγαν ἠδὲ λέβητα
ἀνδρακάς·
sentences.l:
But come, to him let us give a great tripod and a cauldron,
man by man;
sentences.i: But come, let us give him a great tripod and a cauldron, one from each man;
sentences.n: Alcinous makes his proposal. ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’. οἱ is the Homeric dative pronoun ‘to him’. δῶμεν is the aorist subjunctive, first person plural, used as an exhortation: ‘let us give’. τρίποδα and λέβητα are two separate things, a tripod (a three-legged stand or vessel) and a cauldron. ἀνδρακάς is an adverb, ‘man by man’, meaning one set from each of the lords.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δ’ αὖτε ἀγειρόμενοι κατὰ δῆμον
τισόμεθ’·
sentences.l:
and we in turn, gathering throughout the land,
will make ourselves repaid;
sentences.i: and we in our turn will collect throughout the land and repay ourselves;
sentences.n: The cost will be recovered from the people. ἡμεῖς is ‘we’ (the lords), and αὖτε is ‘in turn’. ἀγειρόμενοι is the present middle participle of ἀγείρω ‘gather, collect’. κατὰ δῆμον is ‘throughout the land’; δῆμος names the country and the people who live in it. τισόμεθ’ is the future middle of τίνω ‘pay’; in the middle it means ‘get paid, make pay’, so here ‘recoup ourselves’. The unit begins in the middle of line 14, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἀργαλέον γὰρ ἕνα προικὸς χαρίσασθαι.
sentences.l: for grievous it is for one man to give as a free gift.”
sentences.i: for it is grievous for one man to give a gift with no return.”
sentences.n: The reason for the levy. ἀργαλέον ‘grievous’ is the neuter singular, with ἐστί understood, and the infinitive χαρίσασθαι ‘to give freely, grant as a favour’ is its subject; ἕνα ‘one man’ is the accusative subject of that infinitive. προικός is a genitive used as an adverb, ‘as a free gift, with nothing in return’. The closing quotation mark ends Alcinous’s speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀλκίνοος, τοῖσιν δ’ ἐπιήνδανε μῦθος.
sentences.l: So spoke Alcinous, and to them the word was pleasing.
sentences.i: So spoke Alcinous, and his words pleased them.
sentences.n: The narrator closes the speech with the name filled into the usual ὣς φάτο formula: ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀλκίνοος ‘so spoke Alcinous’. τοῖσιν is the dative plural of the Homeric pronoun, ‘to them’. ἐπιήνδανε is the imperfect of ἐπιανδάνω ‘be pleasing to’, and μῦθος is here Alcinous’s proposal, his ‘word’.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν κακκείοντες ἔβαν οἶκόνδε ἕκαστος,
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
νῆάδ’ ἐπεσσεύοντο, φέρον δ’ εὐήνορα χαλκόν.
sentences.i: They each went off home to bed; and when early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, they hurried to the ship and carried the bronze that is good for men.
sentences.n: Night passes between the end of the speech and the morning’s work. In line 17, κακκείοντες is κατακείοντες ‘wishing to lie down’, with the κατά assimilated to κακ-, and οἶκόνδε is ‘homewards’ (οἶκον + -δε of direction). Line 18 is the formula for dawn: ἠριγένεια ‘early-born’ and ῥοδοδάκτυλος ‘rose-fingered’ are both epithets of Ἠώς. νῆάδ’ is νῆα ‘ship’ (Ionic accusative of νηῦς) with -δε elided: ‘to the ship’. ἐπεσσεύοντο is the imperfect of ἐπισεύομαι ‘hurry to’, and φέρον ‘were carrying’. εὐήνορα is an epithet of bronze (and of wine) whose meaning is not known for certain; it is built from εὖ ‘well, good’ and ἀνήρ ‘man’, and ‘manly, giving manliness’ is the traditional guess. The bronze is the tripods and cauldrons just proposed.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰ μὲν εὖ κατέθηχ’ ἱερὸν μένος Ἀλκινόοιο,
αὐτὸς ἰὼν διὰ νηὸς ὑπὸ ζυγά, μή τιν’ ἑταίρων
βλάπτοι ἐλαυνόντων, ὁπότε σπερχοίατ’ ἐρετμοῖς.
sentences.l:
And these things well put away the sacred strength of Alcinous,
himself going through the ship under the benches, lest any of the companions
it hinder as they rowed, whenever they pressed hard with the oars.
sentences.i: And the sacred strength of Alcinous stowed them well, going himself through the ship beneath the benches, so that they would not hinder any of the companions as they rowed, whenever they strained at the oars.
sentences.n: Alcinous himself supervises the stowing. ἱερὸν μένος Ἀλκινόοιο is a periphrasis for the man, ‘the sacred strength of Alcinous’, as at 24. κατέθηχ’ is κατέθηκε ‘put away’, elided, with the κ aspirated before the rough breathing of ἱερόν. τά is ‘these things’, the gifts. ζυγά are the benches the oarsmen sit on. μή with the optative βλάπτοι ‘lest it hinder’ gives a negative purpose, and the subject (the stowed cargo) is left unstated. ἑταίρων is ‘of the companions’, here the rowers, and ἐλαυνόντων ‘as they rowed’ agrees with it (ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, of rowing). σπερχοίατ’ is the optative of σπέρχομαι ‘press on, hurry’ in the Ionic third plural ending -οίατο; after ὁπότε the optative means ‘whenever’. The μέν here is answered by the δέ of line 23.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ εἰς Ἀλκινόοιο κίον καὶ δαῖτ’ ἀλέγυνον.
sentences.l: And they to Alcinous’ went and the feast prepared.
sentences.i: And they went to Alcinous’ house and made the feast ready.
sentences.n: The δέ answers the μέν of line 20: Alcinous stows the gifts, and the others go to his house. εἰς Ἀλκινόοιο has ‘house’ understood, as English says ‘to the baker’s’. κίον is the past tense of κίω ‘go’ without augment, and ἀλέγυνον is the imperfect of ἀλεγύνω ‘make ready, attend to’. δαῖτα is ‘feast’.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ βοῦν ἱέρευσ’ ἱερὸν μένος Ἀλκινόοιο
Ζηνὶ κελαινεφέϊ Κρονίδῃ, ὃς πᾶσιν ἀνάσσει.
sentences.l:
And for them an ox sacrificed the sacred strength of Alcinous
to Zeus dark-clouded, son of Cronus, who rules over all.
sentences.i: For them the sacred strength of Alcinous sacrificed an ox to Zeus of the dark clouds, the son of Cronus, who rules over all.
sentences.n: The sacrifice is made to Zeus, and Alcinous performs it himself. τοῖσι is ‘for them’. ἱέρευσ’ is the aorist of ἱερεύω ‘sacrifice’. Ζηνί is the dative of Ζεύς. κελαινεφέϊ is the dative of κελαινεφής ‘dark-clouded’ (κελαινός ‘dark’ + νέφος ‘cloud’), the epithet that is translated whenever it appears. Κρονίδῃ is the dative of the patronymic ‘son of Cronus’. ὃς πᾶσιν ἀνάσσει means ‘who is lord over all’ (ἀνάσσω ‘rule’). ἱερὸν μένος Ἀλκινόοιο repeats the periphrasis of line 20.

sentences.t:
μῆρα δὲ κήαντες δαίνυντ’ ἐρικυδέα δαῖτα
τερπόμενοι·
sentences.l:
And the thigh-pieces having burned, they feasted a glorious feast,
delighting;
sentences.i: They burned the thigh-pieces and feasted a glorious feast, enjoying themselves;
sentences.n: The thigh-pieces are the bones wrapped in fat that are burned for the god; the rest of the meat is eaten. κήαντες is the aorist participle of καίω ‘burn’, in its Homeric shape (Attic καύσαντες). δαίνυντ’ is δαίνυντο, the imperfect middle of δαίνυμι ‘feast on’, elided. ἐρικυδέα (ἐρι- intensive + κῦδος ‘glory’) is ‘glorious’, and τερπόμενοι is the present middle participle of τέρπω ‘delight’, here ‘enjoying themselves’. The sentence ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
μετὰ δέ σφιν ἐμέλπετο θεῖος ἀοιδός,
Δημόδοκος, λαοῖσι τετιμένος.
sentences.l:
and among them was making music the divine minstrel,
Demodocus, honoured by the peoples.
sentences.i: and among them the divine minstrel was making music, Demodocus, honoured by the people.
sentences.n: The minstrel of the Phaeacian court, whom Book 8 introduced, performs at the feast. μετά ‘among’ goes with σφιν, the dative plural of the Homeric pronoun, ‘them’. ἐμέλπετο is the imperfect of μέλπομαι ‘celebrate with song (and dance)’, used of the singer’s performance. θεῖος ἀοιδός is ‘the divine minstrel’, the standing phrase. λαοῖσι is a dative of the agent, ‘by the peoples’, and τετιμένος is the perfect passive participle of τιμάω ‘honour’. The unit begins after the ano teleia of line 27 and ends mid-line at the full stop of line 28.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
πολλὰ πρὸς ἠέλιον κεφαλὴν τρέπε παμφανόωντα,
δῦναι ἐπειγόμενος·
sentences.i: But Odysseus kept turning his head toward the all-shining sun, eager for it to set;
sentences.n: The scene shifts from the feast to Odysseus’s impatience. αὐτάρ ‘but’ marks the change. πολλά is used as an adverb, ‘many times, often’. τρέπε is the imperfect of τρέπω ‘turn’, without augment: ‘kept turning’. παμφανόωντα ‘all-shining’ (παν- + φαίνω) is the stretched, uncontracted form of παμφανῶντα, the same lengthening as αἰτιόωνται at 1.32. δῦναι is the infinitive ‘to set’ with the sun as its unstated subject, and ἐπειγόμενος (ἐπείγομαι ‘be eager, press on’) says that Odysseus pressed for it. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 30.

sentences.t: δὴ γὰρ μενέαινε νέεσθαι.
sentences.l: for indeed he was eager to go.
sentences.i: for he was eager to be on his way.
sentences.n: δὴ γάρ is ‘for indeed’, explaining the glances at the sun. μενέαινε is the imperfect of μενεαίνω ‘be eager, long’, which is built on μένος ‘spirit, strength’. νέεσθαι is the uncontracted infinitive of νέομαι ‘go’, usually ‘go home’; the same verb comes again at 61.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἀνὴρ δόρποιο λιλαίεται, ᾧ τε πανῆμαρ
νειὸν ἀν’ ἕλκητον βόε οἴνοπε πηκτὸν ἄροτρον·
sentences.l:
As when a man longs for his supper, whose all day long
through fallow land two wine-faced oxen drag the jointed plough;
sentences.i: As when a man longs for his supper, whose two oxen, with the look of wine, have been dragging the jointed plough through the fallow land all day long;
sentences.n: A simile: Odysseus waiting for sunset is like a ploughman waiting for his evening meal. ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ is ‘as when’. λιλαίεται ‘longs for’ takes the genitive δόρποιο ‘supper’. ᾧ τε is ‘for whom’, with the epic τε. πανῆμαρ is ‘all day long’ (πᾶν ἦμαρ). ἀνά with the accusative νειόν ‘fallow land’ means ‘along, through’. ἕλκητον ‘the two drag’ and βόε οἴνοπε are dual forms: a pair of oxen, οἴνοπε being the dual of οἶνοψ ‘wine-faced’, the word used of the sea, whose exact colour is not known. πηκτόν ‘jointed’ means fastened together.

sentences.t:
ἀσπασίως δ’ ἄρα τῷ κατέδυ φάος ἠελίοιο
δόρπον ἐποίχεσθαι, βλάβεται δέ τε γούνατ’ ἰόντι·
sentences.l:
and gladly for him sank the light of the sun
to go to his supper, and his knees are hurt as he goes;
sentences.i: and with joy for him the light of the sun goes down, so that he may go to his supper, though his knees are sore as he walks;
sentences.n: The simile’s second half: the man’s day ends. ἀσπασίως is ‘gladly’. κατέδυ is an aorist, but in a simile it states what happens every time, so it is rendered as present in the free English. φάος ἠελίοιο is ‘the light of the sun’, with the uncontracted ἠέλιος. ἐποίχεσθαι is the infinitive of ἐποίχομαι ‘go to, go about’. βλάβεται is the passive of βλάπτω ‘hinder, hurt’, with the neuter plural γούνατα ‘knees’ taking a singular verb; ἰόντι is the dative of ἰών ‘going’, ‘as he goes’. δέ τε is the epic τε of what is generally true.

sentences.t: ὣς Ὀδυσῆ’ ἀσπαστὸν ἔδυ φάος ἠελίοιο.
sentences.l: So to Odysseus welcome sank the light of the sun.
sentences.i: So the light of the sun went down, welcome to Odysseus.
sentences.n: The comparison is completed. ὣς ‘so’ answers the ὡς of line 31. Ὀδυσῆ’ is the dative Ὀδυσῆϊ, with elision and one σ. ἀσπαστόν ‘welcome’ is the adjective related to ἀσπασίως ‘gladly’ two lines before, and ἔδυ is the aorist of δύω ‘sink, set’. The words φάος ἠελίοιο repeat line 33, joining the two halves of the simile.

sentences.t:
αἶψα δὲ Φαιήκεσσι φιληρέτμοισι μετηύδα,
Ἀλκινόῳ δὲ μάλιστα πιφαυσκόμενος φάτο μῦθον·
sentences.l:
And at once among the oar-loving Phaeacians he spoke,
and to Alcinous above all making known, he said his word:
sentences.i: And at once he spoke among the oar-loving Phaeacians, and addressing his words above all to Alcinous, he said:
sentences.n: The narrator introduces Odysseus’s farewell. αἶψα is ‘at once’. Φαιήκεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι, and φιληρέτμοισι ‘oar-loving’ (φίλος ‘dear’ + ἐρετμόν ‘oar’) is the Phaeacians’ epithet, which is translated each time. μετηύδα is ‘spoke among’, and the speech is meant for them all. πιφαυσκόμενος is a reduplicated present, ‘making known, declaring’. φάτο is ‘he said’, without augment. μάλιστα is ‘most of all’, and the speech is aimed chiefly at the king.

sentences.t:
Ἀλκίνοε κρεῖον, πάντων ἀριδείκετε λαῶν,
πέμπετέ με σπείσαντες ἀπήμονα, χαίρετε δ’ αὐτοί·
sentences.l:
“Alcinous, lord, most conspicuous of all the people,
send me, having poured libations, unharmed, and be glad yourselves;
sentences.i: “Alcinous, my lord, most distinguished of all the people, send me on my way unharmed, once you have poured libations, and fare well yourselves;
sentences.n: A formal request to be sent home. κρεῖον is the vocative of κρείων ‘lord’, and ἀριδείκετε is the vocative of ἀριδείκετος, the epithet of Alcinous, built from the intensive ἀρι- and a stem meaning ‘show’; the word is rendered ‘most conspicuous’ in the literal English and ‘most distinguished’ in the free English. λαῶν is partitive, ‘of all the peoples’. πέμπετε is an imperative, and σπείσαντες is the aorist participle of σπένδω ‘pour a libation’. ἀπήμονα (ἀ- + πῆμα ‘woe’) agrees with με and means ‘unharmed’. χαίρετε is ‘be glad’, used also as a parting word; the plural addresses all the Phaeacians, and αὐτοί ‘yourselves’ sets them against the departing speaker.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γὰρ τετέλεσται ἅ μοι φίλος ἤθελε θυμός,
πομπὴ καὶ φίλα δῶρα, τά μοι θεοὶ Οὐρανίωνες
ὄλβια ποιήσειαν·
sentences.i: for everything that my heart desired is now accomplished, an escort and dear gifts, and may the gods, the children of Heaven, make them prosper for me;
sentences.n: Odysseus says the Phaeacians have given him all he wanted. ἤδη is ‘already’, and τετέλεσται is the perfect passive of τελέω ‘accomplish’. ἅ is the neuter plural relative ‘the things which’. φίλος θυμός is ‘dear heart’, and ἤθελε is the imperfect of ἐθέλω ‘wish’. πομπή ‘escort’ and φίλα δῶρα ‘dear gifts’ stand in apposition to ἅ, and τά ‘which’ picks them up again. Οὐρανίωνες ‘children of Heaven’ is a name for the gods, either ‘descendants of Uranus’ or ‘dwellers in heaven’. ὄλβια ποιήσειαν is an optative of wish, ‘may they make prosperous’; ὄλβιος is ‘prosperous’.

sentences.t:
ἀμύμονα δ’ οἴκοι ἄκοιτιν
νοστήσας εὕροιμι σὺν ἀρτεμέεσσι φίλοισιν.
sentences.l:
and a blameless wife at home
having returned may I find, with my dear ones sound.
sentences.i: and may I return to find my blameless wife at home, with my dear ones in good health.
sentences.n: The second wish: for his own household. ἀμύμονα ‘blameless’ is the standing epithet and is translated every time, even where it says more than the context asks; what ἀμύμων really means is not known. ἄκοιτιν is the accusative of ἄκοιτις ‘wife’, literally ‘bedfellow’. οἴκοι is ‘at home’ (a locative). νοστήσας is the aorist participle of νοστέω ‘return home’ (from νόστος ‘homecoming’), and εὕροιμι is an optative of wish, ‘may I find’. ἀρτεμέεσσι is an old word, ‘sound, whole’, in the dative plural ending -εσσι, and φίλοισιν are ‘dear ones’, his own people. The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia of line 42.

sentences.t:
ὑμεῖς δ’ αὖθι μένοντες ἐϋφραίνοιτε γυναῖκας
κουριδίας καὶ τέκνα·
sentences.l:
And you, staying here, may you bring joy to your wedded wives
and children;
sentences.i: And as for you, may you stay here and bring joy to your wedded wives and children;
sentences.n: Odysseus’s wish for the Phaeacians. ὑμεῖς is the plural ‘you’. αὖθι is ‘here, on the spot’ (the place suffix -θι), and μένοντες ‘staying’. ἐϋφραίνοιτε is the optative of εὐφραίνω ‘gladden’, a wish. κουριδίας is ‘wedded’, of a wife married as a girl (κούρη). The accusatives γυναῖκας and τέκνα ‘children’ are both objects of ‘gladden’.

sentences.t:
θεοὶ δ’ ἀρετὴν ὀπάσειαν
παντοίην, καὶ μή τι κακὸν μεταδήμιον εἴη.
sentences.l:
and may the gods grant excellence
of every kind, and may there be no evil among the people.”
sentences.i: and may the gods grant you excellence of every kind, and may there be no evil among the people.”
sentences.n: The wish widens to the whole community. ἀρετήν is ‘excellence’, here all kinds of good qualities, and παντοίην is ‘of every kind’. ὀπάσειαν is the aorist optative of ὀπάζω ‘grant, bestow’. μεταδήμιον ‘among the people’ is a compound of μετά ‘among’ and δῆμος ‘land, people’; the same word is said of Hephaestus at 8.293. εἴη is ‘may be’, and μή with the optative gives a negative wish. The closing quotation mark ends Odysseus’s speech to the Phaeacians. The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐπῄνεον ἠδ’ ἐκέλευον
πεμπέμεναι τὸν ξεῖνον, ἐπεὶ κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπεν.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then all praised it and urged
that the stranger be sent, since according to what is fitting he had spoken.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all applauded and urged that the stranger be sent on his way, since he had spoken as was fitting.
sentences.n: The assembled lords approve. ἐπῄνεον is the imperfect of ἐπαινέω ‘approve, applaud’, in uncontracted form, and ἐκέλευον is ‘urged’. πεμπέμεναι is an infinitive in -έμεναι (= πέμπειν) ‘to send’; it states what they urged. τὸν ξεῖνον is ‘the stranger’. κατὰ μοῖραν is ‘according to what is fitting’ (μοῖρα ‘due portion’), and ἔειπεν is the aorist of εἶπον ‘say’.

sentences.t: καὶ τότε κήρυκα προσέφη μένος Ἀλκινόοιο·
sentences.l: And then to the herald addressed the strength of Alcinous:
sentences.i: Then the strength of Alcinous spoke to the herald:
sentences.n: προσέφη is ‘addressed’ (aorist of προσφημί), and μένος Ἀλκινόοιο is again ‘the strength of Alcinous’, the periphrasis for the king. κήρυκα is ‘herald’; he is named in the next line.

sentences.t:
Ποντόνοε, κρητῆρα κερασσάμενος μέθυ νεῖμον
πᾶσιν ἀνὰ μέγαρον, ὄφρ’ εὐξάμενοι Διὶ πατρὶ
τὸν ξεῖνον πέμπωμεν ἑὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.l:
“Pontonous, a mixing-bowl having mixed, wine distribute
to all throughout the hall, so that having prayed to Father Zeus
we may send the stranger to his own fatherland.”
sentences.i: “Pontonous, mix a bowl of wine and serve it to everyone throughout the hall, so that, after praying to Father Zeus, we may send the stranger to his own fatherland.”
sentences.n: Alcinous orders the libation that will close the feast. Ποντόνοε is the vocative of the herald’s name. κρητῆρα is ‘mixing-bowl’, and κερασσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of κεράννυμι ‘mix’ (wine with water). μέθυ is ‘wine’. νεῖμον is the aorist imperative of νέμω ‘distribute’. ὄφρ’ is ‘so that’, εὐξάμενοι is ‘having prayed’, and Διὶ πατρί is ‘to Father Zeus’. πέμπωμεν is ‘we may send’. ἑήν is the possessive ‘his own’ (not the relative), and πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘fatherland’. The first line and a half echo Alcinous’s order to the same herald at 7.179.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Ποντόνοος δὲ μελίφρονα οἶνον ἐκίρνα,
νώμησεν δ’ ἄρα πᾶσιν ἐπισταδόν·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Pontonous the honey-hearted wine mixed,
and dealt it out then to all, standing by each;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Pontonous mixed the heart-sweetening wine and served it out to all, standing by each man;
sentences.n: The herald carries out the order. ὣς φάτο is ‘so he spoke’. ἐκίρνα is the imperfect of κίρνημι ‘mix’ (= κεράννυμι). μελίφρονα is built on μέλι ‘honey’ and φρήν ‘heart’; the sense of the second half is not certain, and ‘heart-sweetening’ is the traditional gloss. νώμησεν is the aorist of νωμάω ‘distribute’, and ἐπισταδόν is ‘standing by (each)’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ θεοῖσιν
ἔσπεισαν μακάρεσσι, τοὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν,
αὐτόθεν ἐξ ἑδρέων.
sentences.l:
and they to the gods
poured libations, the blessed ones, who hold the wide sky,
right there, from their seats.
sentences.i: and they poured libations to the blessed gods, who hold the wide sky, right there from their seats.
sentences.n: The Phaeacians pour libations without leaving their places. οἱ δέ ‘and they’ are the guests. ἔσπεισαν is the aorist of σπένδω. μακάρεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι, ‘blessed’, and τοί is the relative pronoun ‘who’, not the article. οὐρανὸν εὐρύν is ‘the wide sky’. αὐτόθεν is ‘from the very spot’, and ἐξ ἑδρέων is ‘from their seats’ (ἕδρα). The unit starts mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀνὰ δ’ ἵστατο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
Ἀρήτῃ δ’ ἐν χειρὶ τίθει δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And up he stood, heavenly Odysseus,
and in Arete’s hand he placed the double cup,
and, lifting his voice, to her winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Heavenly Odysseus stood up, put the double cup in Arete’s hand, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to her:
sentences.n: Odysseus rises to speak to the queen, and puts the cup into her hand. ἀνὰ δ’ ἵστατο is tmesis for ἀνίστατο ‘stood up’. δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is ‘heavenly Odysseus’. Ἀρήτῃ is the dative of Arete, Alcinous’s wife. τίθει is the imperfect of τίθημι ‘put’. δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον is ‘the double cup’; the exact sense of ἀμφικύπελλον, ‘double’ or ‘two-handled’, is disputed. φωνήσας is ‘having lifted his voice’, and ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is ‘spoke winged words’. The unit starts mid-line, after the full stop.

sentences.t:
χαῖρέ μοι, ὦ βασίλεια, διαμπερές, εἰς ὅ κε γῆρας
ἔλθῃ καὶ θάνατος, τά τ’ ἐπ’ ἀνθρώποισι πέλονται.
sentences.l:
“Be glad, for me, O queen, continually, until old age
and death come, which are upon men.
sentences.i: “Farewell, my queen, all your days, until old age and death come, as they come to all men.
sentences.n: Odysseus’s farewell to Arete. χαῖρε is ‘be glad’, also the word of parting, and μοι is ‘for me’, as if ‘my farewell to you’. ὦ βασίλεια is ‘O queen’. διαμπερές is ‘continually, throughout’. εἰς ὅ κε ‘until’ takes the aorist subjunctive ἔλθῃ, which is singular because it agrees with the nearer subject γῆρας ‘old age’. θάνατος is ‘death’. τά ‘which’, with the epic τε of what is generally true, picks up both; πέλονται is ‘come about, are’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ νέομαι·
sentences.l: But I am going home;
sentences.i: But I am on my way home;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is ‘but’. νέομαι is the present of νέομαι ‘go, go home’, with the sense of a near future; it is the verb of νέεσθαι at 30. The unit is cut at the ano teleia in the middle of line 61.

sentences.t:
σὺ δὲ τέρπεο τῷδ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
παισί τε καὶ λαοῖσι καὶ Ἀλκινόῳ βασιλῆϊ.
sentences.l:
and you, take your delight in this house
with your children and your people and Alcinous the king.”
sentences.i: and you, take your joy in this house with your children, your people, and Alcinous the king.”
sentences.n: τέρπεο is the imperative middle of τέρπω ‘delight’, uncontracted (= τέρπου): ‘take delight’. τῷδ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ is ‘in this house’. παισί, λαοῖσι and Ἀλκινόῳ βασιλῆϊ are datives of association, ‘with’. βασιλῆϊ is the Ionic dative of βασιλεύς. The closing quotation mark ends the farewell.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ὑπὲρ οὐδὸν ἐβήσετο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
τῷ δ’ ἅμα κήρυκα προΐει μένος Ἀλκινόοιο,
ἡγεῖσθαι ἐπὶ νῆα θοὴν καὶ θῖνα θαλάσσης·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and heavenly Odysseus stepped over the threshold, and the strength of Alcinous sent the herald forth with him to lead the way to the swift ship and the shore of the sea;
sentences.n: Odysseus leaves the hall. ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’. ὑπὲρ οὐδὸν ἐβήσετο is ‘stepped over the threshold’, with ἐβήσετο the aorist middle of βαίνω in an intransitive sense. τῷ δ’ ἅμα is ‘and together with him’. προΐει is the imperfect of προΐημι ‘send forth’. ἡγεῖσθαι is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to lead the way’. ἐπὶ νῆα θοήν is ‘to the swift ship’, and θῖνα is the accusative of θίς ‘shore, beach’.

sentences.t:
Ἀρήτη δ’ ἄρα οἱ δμῳὰς ἅμ’ ἔπεμπε γυναῖκας,
τὴν μὲν φᾶρος ἔχουσαν ἐϋπλυνὲς ἠδὲ χιτῶνα,
τὴν δ’ ἑτέρην χηλὸν πυκινὴν ἅμ’ ὄπασσε κομίζειν·
sentences.i: And Arete sent maids with him: one carried a well-washed cloak and a tunic, and to the second she gave a solid chest to carry along;
sentences.n: Arete sends servants with Odysseus’s provisions. δμῳάς is the accusative plural of δμῳή ‘maidservant’, and γυναῖκας ‘women’ stands in apposition. τὴν μέν … τὴν δ’ ἑτέρην is ‘one … the second’. φᾶρος is ‘cloak’ (a man’s cloth, as at 3.467), ἐϋπλυνές is ‘well-washed’, and χιτών is ‘tunic’. χηλόν is ‘chest’, and πυκινήν is ‘solid’. ὄπασσε is the aorist of ὀπάζω ‘give as an escort, assign’; with κομίζειν ‘to carry’ it means ‘gave to carry along’. ἅμ’ is ἅμα ‘together with’.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ ἄλλη σῖτόν τ’ ἔφερεν καὶ οἶνον ἐρυθρόν.
sentences.l: and the other food carried, and red wine.
sentences.i: and another carried food and red wine.
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ ἄλλη is ‘and the other one’, a third woman after the two just described. σῖτον is ‘food’, οἶνον ἐρυθρόν is ‘red wine’, and ἔφερεν is the imperfect of φέρω ‘carry’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἐπὶ νῆα κατήλυθον ἠδὲ θάλασσαν,
αἶψα τά γ’ ἐν νηῒ γλαφυρῇ πομπῆες ἀγαυοὶ
δεξάμενοι κατέθεντο, πόσιν καὶ βρῶσιν ἅπασαν·
sentences.i: And when they had come down to the ship and the sea, the noble escorts received the things and at once stowed them in the hollow ship, all the drink and food;
sentences.n: The party reaches the shore, and the crew takes over. The first line is formulaic for going down to the beach: ῥ’ is ῥα, and κατήλυθον is the aorist of κατέρχομαι ‘come down’. τά γ’ is ‘these things’. πομπῆες is ‘escorts’ (from πομπή), and ἀγαυοί is ‘noble’. δεξάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of δέχομαι ‘receive’, and κατέθεντο is the aorist middle of κατατίθημι ‘put away, stow’. πόσιν ‘drink’ and βρῶσιν ‘food’ explain τά. The ship is γλαφυρῇ ‘hollow’.

sentences.t:
κὰδ δ’ ἄρ’ Ὀδυσσῆϊ στόρεσαν ῥῆγός τε λίνον τε
νηὸς ἐπ’ ἰκριόφιν γλαφυρῆς, ἵνα νήγρετον εὕδοι,
πρυμνῆς·
sentences.i: And for Odysseus they spread a blanket and a linen cloth on the decking of the hollow ship, in the stern, so that he might sleep unwaking;
sentences.n: The sailors prepare a bed for Odysseus. κὰδ … στόρεσαν is tmesis: κατά (written κάδ before δ) + στορέννυμι ‘spread’. ῥῆγος is ‘blanket’, and λίνον ‘linen cloth’. ἰκριόφιν has the old ending -φιν used as a case ending: ‘on the decking’. ἵνα … εὕδοι is purpose with the optative. νήγρετον is made from ν- ‘not’ and ἐγείρω ‘wake’: ‘unwaking’, sleep from which one is not roused. πρυμνῆς ‘hindmost, of the stern’ agrees with νηός: the bed is in the stern part of the ship.

sentences.t:
ἂν δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς ἐβήσετο καὶ κατέλεκτο
σιγῇ·
sentences.l:
and up he himself went and lay down
in silence;
sentences.i: and he himself went aboard and lay down in silence;
sentences.n: ἂν … ἐβήσετο is tmesis again (ἀνεβήσετο ‘went up’), and αὐτός ‘himself’ is Odysseus. κατέλεκτο is the aorist middle of καταλέγω ‘lay oneself down’. σιγῇ is ‘in silence’. The unit starts mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δὲ καθῖζον ἐπὶ κληῗσιν ἕκαστοι
κόσμῳ, πεῖσμα δ’ ἔλυσαν ἀπὸ τρητοῖο λίθοιο.
sentences.l:
and they sat down upon the rowing-benches, each man,
in order, and loosed the cable from the pierced stone.
sentences.i: and they sat down at the oarlocks, each man in his place, and cast off the cable from the pierced stone.
sentences.n: The crew takes its places and the ship casts off. τοί is the pronoun ‘they’. καθῖζον is the imperfect of καθίζω ‘sit down’. κληῗσιν is the dative plural of κληῖς, the rowing-bench or thwart (the English ‘oarlocks’ follows the wording used for this formula elsewhere in the poem). ἕκαστοι is ‘each man’, and κόσμῳ is ‘in order’. πεῖσμα is ‘cable’, and λίθοιο τρητοῖο is ‘the pierced stone’, the mooring stone with a hole bored through it (τρητός ‘bored’). The unit starts mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
εὖθ’ οἱ ἀνακλινθέντες ἀνερρίπτουν ἅλα πηδῷ,
καὶ τῷ νήδυμος ὕπνος ἐπὶ βλεφάροισιν ἔπιπτε,
νήγρετος, ἥδιστος, θανάτῳ ἄγχιστα ἐοικώς.
sentences.l:
And when they, leaning back, tossed up the salt-sea with the oar-blade,
then on him sweet sleep upon his eyelids fell,
unwaking, sweetest, nearest to death in likeness.
sentences.i: And when they leaned back and tossed up the salt sea with the oar, sweet sleep fell on his eyelids, unwaking, the sweetest, most like death.
sentences.n: As the crew rows, Odysseus sleeps. εὖθ’ is εὖτε ‘when’. ἀνακλινθέντες is the aorist passive participle of ἀνακλίνω ‘lean back’, which is the rowers’ movement. ἀνερρίπτουν is the imperfect of ἀναρρίπτω ‘toss up’, and ἅλα is ‘the salt sea’. πηδῷ is a singular dative, ‘with the blade’, for all the oars. νήδυμος ὕπνος is ‘sweet sleep’; the meaning of νήδυμος is not known, and ‘sweet’ is the traditional gloss. βλεφάροισιν is the dative plural of βλέφαρον ‘eyelid’. νήγρετος is ‘unwaking’ (see 74), and ἥδιστος is the superlative of ἡδύς ‘sweet’. ἄγχιστα ‘nearest’ goes with the dative θανάτῳ, and ἐοικώς is the perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’, ὥς τ’ ἐν πεδίῳ τετράοροι ἄρσενες ἵπποι,
πάντες ἅμ’ ὁρμηθέντες ὑπὸ πληγῇσιν ἱμάσθλης,
ὑψόσ’ ἀειρόμενοι ῥίμφα πρήσσουσι κέλευθον,
sentences.l:
And she, as on a plain four-yoked male horses,
all together set in motion under the blows of the lash,
lifting themselves high, nimbly accomplish their way,
sentences.i: As for her, just as four stallions yoked together on a plain all start off at once under the blows of the lash and, rising high, nimbly cover their course,
sentences.n: A long simile for the ship’s speed; the sentence that begins with ἡ δ’ ‘and she’ (the ship) is interrupted by the comparison and resumed in line 84 with τῆς ‘her’, so the construction is loose. ὥς τ’ is ‘as’, with the epic τε. τετράοροι is a rare word usually explained as ‘four-yoked’. ὁρμηθέντες is the aorist passive participle of ὁρμάω, ‘set in motion’. ὑπὸ πληγῇσιν ἱμάσθλης is ‘under the blows of the lash’. ὑψόσ’ is ‘on high’, and ἀειρόμενοι is the middle participle of ἀείρω ‘lift’. ῥίμφα is ‘nimbly’, and πρήσσουσι κέλευθον is ‘accomplish the way’. The main verb πρήσσουσι is present, as in similes generally (ὁρμηθέντες is an aorist participle, ‘having set off’). The unit ends at a comma because the sentence would otherwise run five lines.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα τῆς πρύμνη μὲν ἀείρετο, κῦμα δ’ ὄπισθε
πορφύρεον μέγα θῦε πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης.
sentences.l:
so then her stern was lifted, and behind a wave,
surging, great, rushed, of the much-roaring sea.
sentences.i: so her stern rose, and behind it a great surging wave of the loud-roaring sea came rushing.
sentences.n: The point of the simile: the ship’s stern is lifted and a wave rushes behind. ὣς ‘so’ answers ὥς τ’ in line 81, and τῆς is ‘her’. πρύμνη is ‘stern’, and ἀείρετο is the imperfect passive of ἀείρω ‘lift’. πορφύρεον, said of heaving water, is ‘surging’ (as for a wave at 2.428 and 11.243); here it names motion and sheen, not a plain colour. θῦε is the imperfect of θύω ‘rush, surge’, and πολυφλοίσβοιο is ‘much-roaring’ (πολύς ‘much’ + φλοῖσβος ‘roaring noise’), ‘loud-roaring’ in the free English, an epithet of θάλασσα that is translated each time.

sentences.t: ἡ δὲ μάλ’ ἀσφαλέως θέεν ἔμπεδον·
sentences.l: And she very securely ran, firmly;
sentences.i: She ran on very securely and steadily;
sentences.n: ἡ δέ is ‘and she’, the ship again. μάλ’ is ‘very’, and ἀσφαλέως is ‘securely’. θέεν is the imperfect of θέω ‘run’, without augment, and ἔμπεδον ‘firmly, steadily’ is an adverb. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 86.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κεν ἴρηξ
κίρκος ὁμαρτήσειεν, ἐλαφρότατος πετεηνῶν.
sentences.l:
and not even a hawk, a falcon,
could have kept up with her, the lightest of winged things.
sentences.i: and not even a hawk, a falcon, could have kept pace with her, the lightest of winged things.
sentences.n: οὐδέ κεν … ὁμαρτήσειεν is a potential optative with κεν: ‘could not have kept up’. ὁμαρτέω is ‘keep pace with’. ἴρηξ ‘hawk’ and κίρκος ‘falcon’ stand side by side, and the exact birds cannot be fixed. ἐλαφρότατος is the superlative of ἐλαφρός ‘light, nimble’, and πετεηνῶν is the genitive plural of πετεηνός ‘winged thing, bird’, a partitive genitive.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἡ ῥίμφα θέουσα θαλάσσης κύματ’ ἔταμνεν,
ἄνδρα φέρουσα θεοῖς ἐναλίγκια μήδε’ ἔχοντα·
sentences.l:
So she, nimbly running, cut the waves of the sea,
bearing a man who had counsels like to the gods;
sentences.i: So she, running nimbly, cut through the waves of the sea, carrying a man whose counsels were like the gods’;
sentences.n: ἡ is the ship, ῥίμφα ‘nimbly’, and θέουσα the participle of θέω ‘run’. ἔταμνεν is the imperfect of τάμνω ‘cut’. ἄνδρα φέρουσα is ‘carrying a man’, and the relative clause that follows describes him. θεοῖς ἐναλίγκια is ‘like to the gods’, and μήδε’ is μήδεα ‘counsels, plans’, elided; ἔχοντα agrees with ἄνδρα. The sentence ends at the ano teleia, and the relative clause continues in line 90.

sentences.t:
ὃς πρὶν μὲν μάλα πολλὰ πάθ’ ἄλγεα ὃν κατὰ θυμὸν
ἀνδρῶν τε πτολέμους ἀλεγεινά τε κύματα πείρων,
δὴ τότε γ’ ἀτρέμας εὗδε, λελασμένος ὅσσ’ ἐπεπόνθει.
sentences.l:
who before had suffered very many pains in his own heart,
the wars of men and grievous waves passing through,
but then quietly slept, having forgotten all he had suffered.
sentences.i: He who before had suffered very many pains in his own heart, making his way through the wars of men and the grievous waves, now slept quietly, forgetting everything he had suffered.
sentences.n: The relative clause describing the man of line 89 begins here. πάθ’ is the aorist of πάσχω with its augment missing and its last vowel elided. ὃν κατὰ θυμόν is ‘in his own heart’, the possessive ὅς. πείρων is the participle of πείρω ‘pass through, pierce’. ἀλεγεινά is ‘grievous’. The line ‘the wars of men and grievous waves’ is repeated from 8.183, where Odysseus says it of himself. δὴ τότε γε is ‘but then’, ἀτρέμας ‘quietly, without moving’, and εὗδε ‘was sleeping’. λελασμένος is the perfect middle participle of λανθάνομαι ‘forget’, and ἐπεπόνθει is the pluperfect of πάσχω, ‘had suffered’.

sentences.t:
εὖτ’ ἀστὴρ ὑπερέσχε φαάντατος, ὅς τε μάλιστα
ἔρχεται ἀγγέλλων φάος Ἠοῦς ἠριγενείης,
τῆμος δὴ νήσῳ προσεπίλνατο ποντοπόρος νηῦς.
sentences.l:
When the star rose above, the brightest, which most of all
comes announcing the light of early-born Dawn,
then indeed to the island drew near the sea-crossing ship.
sentences.i: When the brightest star rose, the one that most of all comes announcing the light of early-born Dawn, then the sea-crossing ship drew near the island.
sentences.n: The voyage ends before sunrise. εὖτ’ is ‘when’, and τῆμος ‘then’ answers it. ὑπερέσχε is the aorist of ὑπέρεχω ‘stand over, rise above’. φαάντατος is the superlative of φαεινός, ‘brightest’. ὅς τε μάλιστα is ‘which most of all’, with the epic τε. The star that announces the dawn is the morning star, though the passage does not name it. ἔρχεται ἀγγέλλων is ‘comes announcing’, and Ἠοῦς ἠριγενείης is the genitive of ‘early-born Dawn’. προσεπίλνατο is a compound aorist of πίλναμαι ‘draw near’. ποντοπόρος νηῦς is ‘the sea-crossing ship’. The island is Ithaca, which is named two lines on, at 97.

sentences.t:
Φόρκυνος δέ τίς ἐστι λιμήν, ἁλίοιο γέροντος,
ἐν δήμῳ Ἰθάκης·
sentences.l:
And there is a certain harbour of Phorcys, the old man of the sea,
in the land of Ithaca;
sentences.i: There is a certain harbour of Phorcys, the old man of the sea, in the land of Ithaca;
sentences.n: The poet describes the landing-place. δέ τίς ἐστι is ‘there is a certain’. Φόρκυνος is the genitive of Φόρκυς, a sea-god. ἁλίοιο γέροντος is ‘old man of the sea’ (ἅλιος ‘of the sea’, from ἅλς ‘salt-sea’), the same phrase as is used of Proteus, but without the epithet νημερτής. ἐν δήμῳ Ἰθάκης is ‘in the land of Ithaca’. This is the first time Ithaca is named in this part.

sentences.t:
δύο δὲ προβλῆτες ἐν αὐτῷ
ἀκταὶ ἀπορρῶγες, λιμένος ποτιπεπτηυῖαι,
αἵ τ’ ἀνέμων σκεπόωσι δυσαήων μέγα κῦμα
ἔκτοθεν·
sentences.l:
and two, thrust forward, in it,
headlands, broken-off, crouching toward the harbour,
which ward off the great wave of ill-blowing winds
from outside;
sentences.i: and in it two headlands thrust forward, abruptly broken off and bending toward the harbour, which keep out from outside the great wave raised by ill-blowing winds;
sentences.n: The harbour’s two arms. προβλῆτες is ‘thrust forward’ (from προβάλλω), agreeing with ἀκταί ‘headlands’. ἀπορρῶγες is ‘broken off, abrupt’ (ἀπορρώξ). ποτιπεπτηυῖαι is the perfect participle of ποτιπτήσσω ‘crouch toward’, with the genitive λιμένος: the headlands lean over the harbour. αἵ τ’ is ‘which’, with the epic τε. σκεπόωσι is the stretched form of σκεπάω ‘shelter from, keep off’, the same lengthening as παμφανόωντα at 29. ἀνέμων δυσαήων is ‘of ill-blowing winds’ (δυσ- ‘ill’ + ἄημι ‘blow’), and ἔκτοθεν is ‘from outside’. The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἔντοσθεν δέ τ’ ἄνευ δεσμοῖο μένουσι
νῆες ἐΰσσελμοι, ὅτ’ ἂν ὅρμου μέτρον ἵκωνται.
sentences.l:
and inside, without a tie, stay
well-benched ships, whenever they reach the measure of the anchorage.
sentences.i: while inside, without any cable, well-benched ships lie, whenever they have come to the proper place for mooring.
sentences.n: ἔντοσθεν is ‘inside’, set against ἔκτοθεν. δέ τε is a connective with the epic τε. δεσμοῖο is ‘tie, bond’, here the mooring cable. νῆες ἐΰσσελμοι is ‘well-benched ships’ (ἐΰσσελμος, from σέλμα ‘bench’). ὅτ’ ἂν … ἵκωνται is ‘whenever they reach’, a general clause with the subjunctive. ὅρμου μέτρον is ‘the measure of the anchorage’, that is the point at which a ship can lie at rest. The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὶ κρατὸς λιμένος τανύφυλλος ἐλαίη,
ἀγχόθι δ’ αὐτῆς ἄντρον ἐπήρατον ἠεροειδές,
ἱρὸν νυμφάων αἳ νηϊάδες καλέονται.
sentences.l:
And at the head of the harbour a long-leaved olive,
and near it a lovely cave, misty-looking,
sacred to the nymphs who are called Naiads.
sentences.i: At the head of the harbour stands a long-leaved olive, and near it is a lovely, misty-looking cave sacred to the nymphs who are called Naiads.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is ‘and’ here. ἐπὶ κρατὸς λιμένος is ‘at the head of the harbour’, its inner end. τανύφυλλος is ‘long-leaved’, and ἐλαίη ‘olive’. ἀγχόθι δ’ αὐτῆς is ‘and near it’ (the place suffix -θι), with αὐτῆς the olive. ἄντρον is ‘cave’. ἐπήρατον is ‘lovely, desirable’, from ἔραμαι ‘love’. ἠεροειδές is ‘misty-looking’, built on ἀήρ ‘mist’. ἱρόν is the Ionic form of ἱερόν ‘sacred’, and it governs νυμφάων, the genitive plural of νύμφη. νηϊάδες ‘Naiads’ are nymphs of fresh water, and καλέονται is the uncontracted ‘are called’.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ κρητῆρές τε καὶ ἀμφιφορῆες ἔασιν
λάϊνοι·
sentences.l:
And in it both mixing-bowls and amphorae are
of stone;
sentences.i: Inside are mixing-bowls and jars, all of stone;
sentences.n: ἐν δέ is ‘and in it’. κρητῆρες are ‘mixing-bowls’, and ἀμφιφορῆες ‘jars with a handle at each side’ (ἀμφί ‘both sides’ + φέρω). ἔασιν is the epic third plural of εἰμί. λάϊνοι is ‘of stone’ (λᾶας ‘stone’).

sentences.t: ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτα τιθαιβώσσουσι μέλισσαι.
sentences.l: and there then the bees make their nests.
sentences.i: and there the bees have their hives.
sentences.n: ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτα is ‘and there then’. τιθαιβώσσουσι is a rare verb whose sense is taken from the context, ‘nest, make their hives’. μέλισσαι are ‘bees’. The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἱστοὶ λίθεοι περιμήκεες, ἔνθα τε νύμφαι
φάρε’ ὑφαίνουσιν ἁλιπόρφυρα, θαῦμα ἰδέσθαι·
sentences.l:
And in it looms of stone, very long, where the nymphs
weave cloths sea-purple, a wonder to see;
sentences.i: There are looms of stone, very long, where the nymphs weave sea-purple cloths, a wonder to behold;
sentences.n: ἱστοί are looms; the same word means ‘mast’ elsewhere (it is the upright pole in both). λίθεοι is ‘of stone’, and περιμήκεες ‘very long’. ἔνθα τε is ‘where’, with the epic τε. φάρε’ is φάρεα ‘cloths’, elided (the word φᾶρος ‘cloak’ of line 67), and ὑφαίνουσιν is ‘weave’. ἁλιπόρφυρα is ‘sea-purple’ (ἅλς ‘salt sea’ + πορφύρεος ‘purple’): cloth of the sea’s colour. θαῦμα ἰδέσθαι is ‘a wonder to see’, the infinitive saying in what respect.

sentences.t: ἐν δ’ ὕδατ’ ἀενάοντα.
sentences.l: and in it waters ever-flowing.
sentences.i: and in it are ever-flowing waters.
sentences.n: ὕδατ’ is ὕδατα, the neuter plural of ὕδωρ ‘water’. ἀενάοντα is ‘ever-flowing’, from ἀεί ‘always’ and a verb of flowing. The unit ends at the full stop in the middle of line 109.

sentences.t:
δύω δέ τέ οἱ θύραι εἰσίν,
αἱ μὲν πρὸς Βορέαο καταιβαταὶ ἀνθρώποισιν,
αἱ δ’ αὖ πρὸς Νότου εἰσὶ θεώτεραι·
sentences.i: And the cave has two doors; one, toward the North Wind, is a way down for men, the other, toward the South Wind, is more divine;
sentences.n: δύω is ‘two’. οἱ is the dative ‘to it’ and shows possession: ‘it has’. αἱ μέν … αἱ δ’ is ‘the one … the other’. πρὸς Βορέαο is ‘toward the North Wind’ and πρὸς Νότου ‘toward the South Wind’, the winds standing for directions. καταιβαταί is ‘to be gone down by’, from καταβαίνω. ἀνθρώποισιν is ‘for men’. θεώτεραι is the comparative of θεῖος ‘divine’: ‘more divine’. The unit begins mid-line, after the full stop.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι κείνῃ
ἄνδρες ἐσέρχονται, ἀλλ’ ἀθανάτων ὁδός ἐστιν.
sentences.l:
and by that one
no men enter, but it is the way of the immortals.
sentences.i: and by that one no men go in; it is the way of the immortals.
sentences.n: οὐδέ τι is ‘not at all’. κείνῃ is ἐκείνῃ ‘by that way’. ἐσέρχονται is ‘enter’, and ἄνδρες ‘men’. ἀθανάτων ὁδός is ‘the way of the immortals’, and ὁδός means ‘road, path’. The last line of the part describes the cave’s second door, which men do not use. The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia.
